title: Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph
directAnswer: Count the isolated 'islands' of nodes in an undirected graph. Either flood each unvisited node with DFS/BFS and count how many floods you launch, or use Union-Find: start with n components and decrement the count once per edge that joins two previously-separate groups. The optimal answer is Union-Find with path compression + union by rank — near O(n + e·α(n)).

remember.pattern: Connected-components count via DFS flood or Union-Find
remember.formula:
Union-Find:
count = n
for (a, b) in edges:
    if find(a) != find(b): union(a, b); count--
return count
# count drops only on a SUCCESSFUL union (different roots)
rules: Start the component count at **n** (every node its own island) and **decrement once per successful union** — never on an edge whose endpoints already share a root.
Build an **adjacency list** for the DFS version — edges come as a pair list, not an adjacency structure, so convert first.
DFS/BFS: count a new component **only when you start a flood** from an unvisited node; mark visited as you go to avoid recounting.
Union-Find needs **path compression AND union by rank/size** to get near-O(1) per op — skipping either degrades toward O(n) find chains.
The graph is **undirected**, so each edge `[a,b]` connects both ways — add both directions in the adjacency list.
whenToUse: Count groups / islands / clusters in an undirected graph
Dynamic connectivity — edges arrive and you ask 'same group?' repeatedly
Detect whether adding an edge creates a cycle (endpoints already connected)
Merge-as-you-go problems (accounts merge, friend circles, Kruskal's MST)
antiSignals: Directed graph + reachability → that's SCCs (Tarjan/Kosaraju), not plain components
Need the actual shortest path between nodes → BFS/Dijkstra, not component counting
Single connectivity query, no merging → a plain DFS/BFS is simpler than DSU
Weighted MST asked, not a count → Union-Find is a building block but the answer is the tree, not the component count
remember.takeaway: Connected components is the 'hello world' of Union-Find: n disjoint sets, one decrement per genuine merge. Once you internalise 'count = n minus the number of successful unions', you'll reuse the same DSU for Redundant Connection, Accounts Merge, Number of Provinces, and Kruskal's MST.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognise a counting-groups problem maps to either graph traversal or a disjoint-set structure, and whether you can implement Union-Find correctly — especially decrementing the count only on a real merge.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Decrementing the component count on every edge instead of only when find(a) != find(b), which undercounts whenever an edge connects two already-joined nodes.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Offer both: DFS for clarity, Union-Find for dynamic connectivity. Mention path compression + union by rank give near-constant amortised ops (inverse Ackermann), and that 'count = n − successful unions' is the invariant.

problemStatement:
You have a graph of `n` nodes labelled from `0` to `n - 1`. You are given an integer `n` and an array `edges` where `edges[i] = [aᵢ, bᵢ]` indicates that there is an **undirected** edge between nodes `aᵢ` and `bᵢ` in the graph.

Return ***the number of connected components*** in the graph.
understanding: Picture the nodes as dots and edges as strings tying some dots together. A connected component is one clump you could lift off the table as a single piece. We just need to count the clumps — including lone dots with no strings attached.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are isolated nodes counted as components?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — a node with no edges is its own component of size one. That's why the count starts at n in the Union-Find version.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the graph directed?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No, undirected. Each edge connects both ways, so in the adjacency list I add a→b and b→a.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can there be duplicate edges or self-loops?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The constraints say no repeated edges and aᵢ ≠ bᵢ. But a robust Union-Find handles both gracefully — a duplicate edge is just a union that finds equal roots and does nothing.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do you want DFS or Union-Find?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Both work in near-linear time. DFS is more readable; Union-Find shines when edges stream in and you need repeated connectivity queries. I'll present both and implement Union-Find as the optimal.

examples.explanation: Nodes {0,1,2} form one component and {3,4} form another → 2 components.
All five nodes are chained together into a single component.
No edges, so every node is its own isolated component.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Decision tree for component counting. This problem fits either branch; Union-Find wins for dynamic connectivity.

approaches.name: DFS Flood From Each Unvisited Node
approaches.whenToMention: The intuitive first answer — say it to show you see the graph traversal, then offer Union-Find for the dynamic-connectivity follow-up.
hints: If you start at a node and walk every edge you can reach, you've discovered one entire component. How many times do you have to RESTART that walk to cover the whole graph?
Build an adjacency list from the edge pairs (both directions, it's undirected). Keep a visited array.
Loop over all n nodes; each time you hit an unvisited one, increment a counter and DFS-flood everything reachable from it, marking visited. The counter is the answer.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Building the adjacency list is O(e); the DFS visits each node once and traverses each edge twice (both directions) → O(n + e) time. Adjacency list O(n + e), visited array and recursion stack O(n) → O(n + e) space.
approaches.explanation:
Treat each component as a region to flood-fill. Walk every node; whenever you find one you haven't seen, that's a brand-new component, so bump the count and flood everything reachable from it.

**Why one flood equals one component.** A DFS (or BFS) launched from a node visits exactly the set of nodes reachable from it — which is precisely its connected component. So the number of *times you have to start a fresh flood* is the number of components. Marking nodes visited as you go guarantees you never start a second flood inside a component you've already counted.

**Why you must convert edges to an adjacency list first.** The input is a flat list of pairs — great for Union-Find, useless for DFS, which needs to ask 'who are node x's neighbours?' in O(1). Since the graph is undirected, each edge `[a,b]` goes into both `adj[a]` and `adj[b]`; forgetting the second direction silently splits components in two.

**Why it's clean but not always ideal.** It's O(n + e) and very readable. The limitation is that it answers one static snapshot — if edges arrive over time and you keep asking 'are these two connected now?', you'd re-flood repeatedly. That dynamic-connectivity scenario is exactly where Union-Find pulls ahead.
approaches.insight: Component counting reduces to 'how many independent flood-fills cover the graph?'. The visited array is what makes each component get counted exactly once — it's the same trick as Number of Islands, just on an explicit graph instead of a grid.

dryRun.intro: adj = {0:[1], 1:[0,2], 2:[1], 3:[4], 4:[3]}. Each fresh flood is one component.

diagrams.title: Visited array filling per flood
diagrams.caption: Flood from node 0 covers {0,1,2}; flood from node 3 covers {3,4}.

edgeCases.behavior: No edges → every node is unvisited when reached → 4 separate floods → 4.

pitfalls: Adding only one direction per edge — undirected graph gets split, overcounting components.
Incrementing count inside the DFS instead of in the outer loop — counts nodes, not components.
Deep recursion on a long chain can overflow the stack — use an explicit stack / BFS for very large n.

approaches.name: Union-Find with Path Compression + Union by Rank (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer for dynamic connectivity. Frame it as 'start with n islands, merge once per real edge, count the merges' and mention the two optimisations by name.
hints: Forget traversal. Start by assuming all n nodes are separate islands — count = n. What happens to the count each time an edge genuinely joins two different islands?
Use a disjoint-set (Union-Find): parent[] array, find(x) follows parents to the root, union(a,b) links one root under the other. Decrement count only when find(a) != find(b).
Add path compression (point nodes straight at the root during find) and union by rank (attach the shorter tree under the taller). Together they give near-constant amortised operations.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each of the e edges does two finds and maybe a union; with path compression + union by rank, each operation is amortised α(n) (inverse Ackermann ≈ constant). Plus O(n) init → O(n + e·α(n)) time, O(n) for the parent and rank arrays.
approaches.explanation:
Model connectivity directly with a disjoint-set forest. Every node starts as its own root (n components); each edge tries to merge its two endpoints, and the count drops by one only when the merge actually joins two distinct sets.

**Why 'count = n − successful unions' is the whole algorithm.** Initially nothing is connected, so there are n components. Joining two *separate* components reduces the total by exactly one. Joining two nodes that are *already* in the same component changes nothing (it'd be a redundant edge / cycle). So if you decrement only on a successful union — when `find(a) != find(b)` — the running count is always the exact number of components. Decrementing on every edge is the classic bug; it undercounts whenever the graph has a cycle.

**Why path compression matters.** `find(x)` walks parent pointers up to the root. Without compression those chains can grow to length n, making find O(n). Path compression re-points every node on the path directly to the root as it returns, so future finds on those nodes are O(1). It flattens the tree opportunistically, for free, during queries you were doing anyway.

**Why union by rank matters.** When merging two trees, attach the *shorter* one under the *taller* one's root. This keeps trees shallow — height grows only when two equal-rank trees merge. Combined with path compression, the amortised cost per operation is the inverse Ackermann function α(n), which is ≤ 4 for any input you'll ever see — effectively constant.

**Why it beats DFS here.** Same near-linear cost on a static graph, but Union-Find is *incremental*: feed edges one at a time and it maintains the component count and answers 'connected?' in near-O(1) without ever re-traversing. That's why it's the canonical answer for dynamic-connectivity and cycle-detection variants.
approaches.insight: Union-Find turns 'are these in the same group, and how many groups are there?' into two near-constant operations. The mental model is a forest of trees where each tree is a component and its root is the component's id; the two optimisations exist solely to keep those trees pancake-flat so find never walks far.

dryRun.intro: Start count=5, each node its own root. Decrement only when the two endpoints have different roots.

java.line: for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) parent[i] = i;
java.explanation: Every node is its own root — n separate components to start.
The invariant: count = n minus the number of successful unions.
Only a merge of DISTINCT sets reduces the component count — this guard is the whole correctness.
Path compression (halving): skip nodes to their grandparent, flattening the tree as we climb.
Decrement exactly once per genuine merge.

python.explanation: parent[i] = i: each node starts as its own root.
Path compression by halving — keeps find near O(1).
Different roots = a real merge; same root = redundant edge, count unchanged.
Union by rank: ensure ra is the taller root so the shorter tree attaches under it.
One decrement per successful union maintains the invariant.

diagrams.title: Disjoint-set forest after all unions
diagrams.caption: Two trees remain — {0,1,2} rooted at 0 and {3,4} rooted at 3 — so count ended at 2.

edgeCases.behavior: First two unions drop count 3→2→1; edge [0,2] finds equal roots → no decrement → 1. This is the cycle case the find-check guards against.
No edges → no unions → count stays 4.

pitfalls: Decrementing count on every edge instead of only when find(a) != find(b) — undercounts on cycles.
Omitting path compression or union by rank — find chains degrade toward O(n), losing the near-constant guarantee.
Recursive find without compression on a long chain — slow and risks stack overflow for large n.

commonMistakes: Decrementing the component count on every edge rather than only on a successful union.
Adding just one direction per undirected edge in the DFS adjacency list, splitting components.
Skipping path compression / union by rank, so Union-Find degrades to near-O(n) per operation.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Decrementing on every edge
commonMistakesDetailed.why: An edge between two nodes already in the same component must NOT reduce the count. Decrementing unconditionally undercounts every time the graph contains a cycle or a duplicate edge.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
count = n
for a, b in edges:
    union(a, b)
    count -= 1          # wrong: also fires on redundant edges
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
count = n
for a, b in edges:
    ra, rb = find(a), find(b)
    if ra != rb:        # only a genuine merge
        union(ra, rb)
        count -= 1

commonMistakesDetailed.title: One-directional adjacency list
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The graph is undirected, so edge [a,b] must appear in both adj[a] and adj[b]. Adding only adj[a] makes the DFS unable to reach a from b, splitting a single component into two.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Find without path compression
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A plain find that walks parents to the root can traverse an O(n) chain on a skewed tree, making the whole algorithm O(n·e). Compressing the path during find keeps subsequent lookups near O(1).

followupVariations.title: Redundant Connection
followupVariations.hint: Use Union-Find to find the edge whose endpoints already share a root — that edge closes the cycle.

followupVariations.title: Number of Islands
followupVariations.hint: Connected components on a grid — DFS flood or Union-Find over cells.

followupVariations.title: Graph Valid Tree
followupVariations.hint: A tree is exactly one component with n−1 edges and no cycle — Union-Find checks both at once.

patternNote: Canonical Disjoint-Set Union (Union-Find). Recognise it whenever you count groups, test dynamic connectivity, or detect cycles in an undirected graph — n disjoint sets, merge on each real edge. Same engine behind Number of Provinces, Redundant Connection, Accounts Merge, and Kruskal's MST.
